idiom_name: FXML document as the presentational half; @FXML-injected controller with observable properties as the supply half
implementation_notes: In JavaFX the presentational half is the FXML document: nodes are declared in markup and bind to observable properties instead of looking anything up. The supply half is the controller class, whose @FXML-annotated fields and handler methods the loader injects; it obtains the data, exposes it as properties and keeps the nodes passive (textProperty().bind(model.totalProperty().asString())). What replaces hand-written container plumbing is loader injection plus property binding - the markup can be replaced without touching Java, and the controller can be tested with a stub model. This is the default Java realization; the Swing variant covers applications that predate it.
pitfalls: In a named module the controller package must be opened to javafx.fxml (`opens <pkg> to javafx.fxml`), otherwise the loader fails at runtime with InaccessibleObjectException.
JavaFX is not part of the JDK from Java 11 on: it is a separate OpenJFX dependency, so a build that works on a bundled JDK can fail on a plain one.
Long-running work in a handler blocks the JavaFX application thread; the supply half should move it to a Task and publish the result.

variants.name: Swing: JPanel as supply half, passive child components
variants.idiom_name: JPanel subclass owning the model and wiring; child components as passive displays
variants.implementation_notes: Swing has no markup layer, so the split is written in code: a JPanel subclass is the classic supply half - it owns the model, wires listeners and pushes values into child components, while the children display what they are set to and fire events (the Swing tutorial's own ConversionPanel coordinates its children exactly this way). Where a large data set is involved, Swing's model/view split (a ListModel or TableModel with a passive JList or JTable) plays the same role: the model supplies, the component renders. Keep this variant for existing Swing applications and desktop tooling; new Java UI work normally starts from the JavaFX variant.
pitfalls: Component mutations must happen on the event dispatch thread; call SwingUtilities.invokeLater from background work or the component tree can end up inconsistent.
A child component that reads the model itself, or a model shared across windows, reintroduces the coupling the split removes.
Deeply nested panels with repeated revalidation make redraws expensive; keep the child hierarchy shallow and reuse components.
